title: What Does Jeremiah 29:11 Really Mean?
subtitle: A promise to prosper, first sent to exiles told to build houses and settle in for seventy years. What it meant in Babylon, what it means now, and what it never promised.

sections.title: The Verse on the Refrigerator
sections.body:
"For I know the plans I have for you, declares the LORD, plans to prosper you and not to harm you, to give you a future and a hope." That's Jeremiah 29:11 in the Berean Standard Bible, and people tend to meet it a long way from the book of Jeremiah. It comes on graduation cards and framed prints over a child's bed. It gets written on the flyleaf of a Bible given to a teenager, and it gets taped to refrigerators in the kind of year nobody would choose.

People reach for this verse for good reasons, and those reasons deserve to be named first. It tells you that God knows. He has intentions toward you, not merely reactions, and his intentions are good. It speaks of a future to people who can't see one. When the test results come back wrong, or the house is suddenly too quiet, a person needs to hear that the story isn't over and that someone is still holding the pen. This verse says so in God's own voice, and it says it tenderly.

The person who keeps this verse on the refrigerator is not the problem, and nothing in this guide is meant to take it down. If the verse has been shrunk, the shrinking wasn't done by the people who love it. It was done by those of us who were supposed to teach them the chapter and handed them a sentence instead. I'm a pastor, so that indictment has my name in it.

The chapter is harder than the card. It's also sturdier, sturdy enough to carry years the card was never built to hold.

sections.title: A Letter to Babylon
sections.body:
The verse sits inside "the letter that Jeremiah the prophet sent from Jerusalem to the surviving elders among the exiles and to the priests, the prophets, and all the others Nebuchadnezzar had carried into exile from Jerusalem to Babylon" (Jeremiah 29:1). The next verse fixes the moment. King Jeconiah, also called Jehoiachin, had been taken to Babylon with the queen mother, the court, and the city's craftsmen, in the deportation many scholars date to 597 BC. Jerusalem itself was still standing; it would fall about a decade later. The exiles had been carried hundreds of miles from the temple and the land, and the question beneath every other question was how soon they could go home.

Jeremiah's answer comes before our verse, and it isn't the one they wanted. "Build houses and settle down. Plant gardens and eat their produce" (29:5). Marry, raise children, and find spouses for those children. Then comes the most startling command in the letter: "Seek the prosperity of the city to which I have sent you as exiles. Pray to the LORD on its behalf, for if it prospers, you too will prosper" (29:7). This was the empire that had taken their king.

A warning follows. Prophets among the exiles were promising a short stay, and in the chapter just before, a prophet named Hananiah had announced in the temple that within two years Babylon's yoke would be broken and the king and the exiles brought home (28:2-4). God's word on such prophets is blunt: "I have not sent them, declares the LORD" (29:9). Then the timetable: "When Babylon's seventy years are complete, I will attend to you and confirm My promise to restore you to this place" (29:10). Only then comes the verse on the refrigerator, and after it the promise that they will call on God and find him (29:12-14). The letter's opponents understood it. One exile, Shemaiah, wrote to the priests in Jerusalem complaining that Jeremiah had written to the exiles, "Since the exile will be lengthy, build houses and settle down" (29:28).

sections.title: Seventy Years and a Plural You
sections.body:
Two details in the letter change how the verse sounds. The first is grammar. In Hebrew, every you in verses 10 through 14 is plural. God is speaking to a people, and the plans he knows are plans for them together. The second is arithmetic. "The length of our days is seventy years," says Psalm 90:10, and the letter itself plans for grandchildren: "Take wives for your sons and give your daughters in marriage, so that they too may have sons and daughters" (29:6). A promise with that horizon, spoken to grown men and women, implied that many of them would be buried in Babylon and that the road home would belong to their children and grandchildren.

The exiles had reason to believe God was finished with them. Ezekiel, himself an exile, records what the people still in Jerusalem were saying about the deported: "They are far away from the LORD; this land has been given to us as a possession" (Ezekiel 11:15). Jeremiah's letter answers from God's side. Their exile was not God's absence, since he calls Babylon "the city to which I have sent you as exiles" (29:7). His intentions toward them were shalom, the Hebrew word behind prosper in verse 11 and behind the prosperity of Babylon they were told to seek in verse 7. He could be found far from the temple: "You will seek Me and find Me when you search for Me with all your heart" (29:13). And right after the verse, the letter turns hard toward those who stayed in Jerusalem (29:16-19). The future went into exile with the people who had lost everything.

The promise was kept. The book of Ezra opens with Cyrus's proclamation, which came "to fulfill the word of the LORD spoken through Jeremiah" (Ezra 1:1). It was spoken to a people, and it was kept to a people.

sections.title: What It Promises Now, and What It Doesn't
sections.body:
How does a promise made to Judah's exiles reach a Christian twenty-six centuries later? Not by pretending the letter was addressed to us. It reaches us as every promise of God does: "For all the promises of God are 'Yes' in Christ" (2 Corinthians 1:20). Peter addresses scattered believers as "the elect who are exiles of the Dispersion" (1 Peter 1:1) and, two verses later, speaks of "a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead" (1 Peter 1:3). The letter was Judah's first, and it was kept to Judah first. The church reads it as a younger sibling reads a letter written to an older one, learning how God treats his people in a land that isn't home.

Read that way, the verse still promises a great deal. God hasn't abandoned his people wherever they've been carried, and his intentions toward them are shalom even when every circumstance argues otherwise. He lets himself be found by those who seek him with the whole heart, and his future for them is larger than one lifetime.

What it doesn't promise matters as much. A personal career path is nowhere in it; E. Randolph Richards and Brandon O'Brien use this very verse to show how Western readers hear a promise to a community as a promise to one person. A quick rescue isn't in it either; the letter was written to refute that hope. Nor is money. The English word prosper has drifted toward wealth, and prosperity teaching has been glad to let it drift, but shalom means wholeness and welfare, and here the exiles' shalom was bound up with the good of a pagan city.

The misreadings run in both political directions, each keeping the part of the letter that suits it. The temptation on the right is to let a nation read itself into the you of this verse and hear restored greatness on a short schedule, which was Hananiah's sermon. On the left, it is to keep verse 7 as a civic program and quietly drop the God the exiles were told to seek. I can find both edits in my own heart. The skeptic who finds the graduation-card version too easy is right, and Jeremiah agrees with him.

sections.title: Praying It in Babylon
sections.body:
So keep the verse, on the refrigerator if that's where it lives. But read it with its neighbors, and let them change the way you pray it.

Pray it in the plural. Ask for the future God promised on behalf of your church, the believers in places you'll never see, and the generation that will outlive you. That is the use it was written for. Pray for the place where you actually live, including people in it you'd rather not bless, because the letter ties the exiles' welfare to Babylon's. James Davison Hunter drew on this letter for what he called faithful presence, his alternative to a habit the right and the left share: trying to change the world chiefly through political power.

Build and plant as though you're staying, because in the ways that matter you are: put down roots, keep your promises, do honest work, and do it for a harvest someone else may gather. And seek God rather than the plan. Verses 13 and 14 don't promise that you'll find your way. They promise that you'll find him: "I will be found by you, declares the LORD" (29:14).

The book of Daniel shows an exile reading Jeremiah's seventy years. Daniel "understood from the sacred books, according to the word of the LORD to Jeremiah the prophet, that the desolation of Jerusalem would last seventy years," and he answered the arithmetic with prayer: "So I turned my attention to the Lord God to seek Him by prayer and petition, with fasting, sackcloth, and ashes" (Daniel 9:2-3). What follows is a long confession of his people's sin, with himself inside it. Reading the promise sent him to repentance.

That is how the verse asks to be kept. It won't tell you when. It asks you to build and plant and pray in a place that isn't home, for neighbors who may never thank you and people you may not live to meet. What it promises is that the God who sent his people into Babylon was already planning their return. Christians hold that promise from the far side of an empty tomb, where a future larger than one lifetime is no longer a figure of speech. A hope that outlives you is still a hope for you.
